subject: latent seasonality not correlated with x

messages.author: 3444f9129095f179
messages.subject: latent seasonality not correlated with x
parts:
I would like to model a latent weekly seasonality which is not too correlated (orthogonal) with my x (IV) variables. 

y <- normal(x * beta + b*seas, sigma)

2 questions

1. is there an easy way to write weekly seasonality in stan: I have seen seas[t] <- -seas[t-1] - .... seas[t-52] but writing out 52 terms seems inefficient
2. how can I specify the model so that the cov() between all x variables and latent seas is minimised

Dirk

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] latent seasonality not correlated with x
parts:
> On May 16, 2016, at 7:36 AM, 'Dirk Nachbar' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> I would like to model a latent weekly seasonality which is not too correlated (orthogonal) with my x (IV) variables.
>
> y <- normal(x * beta + b*seas, sigma)

I assume you meant to define a likelihood here with

y ~

Assignment (<-) is different in Stan.

>
> 2 questions
>
> 1. is there an easy way to write weekly seasonality in stan: I have seen seas[t] <- -seas[t-1] - .... seas[t-52] but writing out 52 terms seems inefficient
This definition doesn't ground out. What's the full definition?
> 2. how can I specify the model so that the cov() between all x variables and latent seas is minimised

There's no minimization going on in Bayesian modeling. Your
likelihood determines one term for seas and the prior will determine
the other, and then you just turn the crank to get the posterior.

If you optimize, you'll fit beta and seas to minimize negative log
likelihood; or in the case of a simple normal, least squares.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] latent seasonality not correlated with x
parts:
Double exponential is a proper desnity, so it doesn't have
flat tails.

Yes, you can define a covariance matrix in transformed parameters
that has some zero elements and some varying elements. Maintaining
positive-definiteness is the tricky part. You don't want to just
be rejecting because HMC will reduce to a very inefficient rejection
sampler.
> See this example for a daily seasonality http://tjo-en.hatenablog.com/entry/2015/08/18/123000

Thanks for linking to the blog (love your icon, by the way).

In the linked blog entry, you want to make sure you use <lower=0> with
all of your scale parameters (s_trend, etc.) --- they need to be > 0.

I didn't understand why you set the model up the way you did. But
this

season[i]~normal(-season[i-1]
- season[i-2]
- season[i-3]
- season[i-4]
- season[i-5]
- season[i-6], s_season);

is more efficiently (and compactly) coded as:

season[i] ~ normal(-sum(season[(i-6):(i-1)]), s_season);

And if you declare your variables as vectors rather than arrays, you can
vectorize this

for (i in 1:N)
q[i]~normal(a*x1[i]+b*x2[i]+c*x3[i]+d,s_q);

as

q ~ normal(a * x1 + b * x2 + c * x3 + d, s_q);

That should help quite a bit with speed.

- Bob

P.S. Please don't use tabs in code --- they render differently
on different platforms.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] latent seasonality not correlated with x
parts:
One more thing for efficiency. When you have
parameter fits like these,

> a_est2
[1] 0.0001505969

> b_est2
[1] 0.0002937902

> c_est2
[1] 5.39804e-05

> d_est2
[1] 1516.145

it's bad news for Stan's adaptation, becuase it has to span 8
orders of magnitude. It's much better if all parameters
are as close to normal(0, 1) as possible in their posteriors.
Scaling whatever the predictors are will help with this.

It makes a huge difference for efficiency of adaptation.

- Bob
